title: What an eigenvector does
summary: Multiply one 2×2 matrix by three vectors, see which ones only get stretched, and read off the stretch.

blocks.title: A times (1, 1)
blocks.why: A matrix moves vectors around. Most vectors get turned; a few only get stretched. Start by watching what this one does.

slips.say: That is only the first column of $A$. $(1, 1)$ takes one of each column: add both columns.

hints: Each entry of $A\,(1, 1)$ is one row of $A$ dotted with $(1, 1)$.

check.say: Dotting a row with $(1, 1)$ just adds up that row. So each entry is a row sum of $A$.

blocks.solution: $(3, 3) = 3\,(1, 1)$: same direction, three times as long. $A$ only stretched it.

blocks.title: A times (1, −1)
blocks.why: A second direction to test. Watch whether the answer still points along the vector you started with.

slips.say: Row 2 is $(1, 2)$, so its entry is $1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot (-1) = 1 - 2$.
The minus sign was dropped: that is $A\,(1, 1)$ again. The second entry of the vector is $-1$.

hints: Same as before: each entry is a row of $A$ dotted with the vector.

check.say: Is your answer a number times $(1, -1)$? Its two entries should be equal and opposite.

blocks.solution: $(1, -1) = 1 \cdot (1, -1)$: $A$ left this direction exactly as it was. A stretch by 1 still counts as only stretching.

blocks.title: A times (1, 0)
blocks.why: Now a vector that is not special, to see what "turned" looks like.

slips.say: That is the second column of $A$. $(1, 0)$ picks out the first column.

hints: $A$ times $(1, 0)$ takes one of the first column and none of the second.
So the answer is a column of $A$. Which one?

check.say: It should equal the first column of $A$.

blocks.solution: $(2, 1)$ is not a multiple of $(1, 0)$: its second entry is not 0. $A$ turned this vector, so it is not one of the special ones.

blocks.title: The stretch factor

define.meaning: A non-zero vector $v$ that $A$ only stretches: $Av = \lambda v$ for some number $\lambda$. The zero vector never counts.
The number $\lambda$ in $Av = \lambda v$: how much $A$ stretches that eigenvector. It may be 1, 0 or negative.

blocks.why: Eigenvectors are the directions a matrix keeps. The eigenvalue says what it does along each one, and that is most of what the matrix does.
blocks.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$: $A\,(1, 1) = (3, 3)$ and $A\,(1, -1) = (1, -1)$. Give the eigenvalue for each vector.
hints: $\lambda$ is the number that turns $v$ into $Av$.
Compare first entries: $\lambda$ times the first entry of $v$ is the first entry of $Av$.

check.say: Multiply each vector by your $\lambda$. You should get $Av$ back, in both entries.

blocks.solution: $A$ stretches $(1, 1)$ by 3 and leaves $(1, -1)$ alone. Every other direction gets turned, as $(1, 0)$ did.

blocks.title: Which are eigenvectors?
blocks.why: Being an eigenvector is about direction, not about length. This tests that, and the one exception.

options.say: Right. $A\,(3, 3) = (9, 9) = 3\,(3, 3)$. It is $3\,(1, 1)$, so it lies on the same line and has the same eigenvalue.
Right. $A\,(5, -5) = (5, -5)$, eigenvalue 1, the same as for $(1, -1)$.
Not this one. $A\,(0, 0) = (0, 0)$ for every matrix, so it would make every number an eigenvalue. The zero vector is ruled out by definition.
Not this one. $A\,(1, 0) = (2, 1)$, which points somewhere else: $A$ turned it.
Not this one. $A\,(1, 2) = (4, 5)$, and no number times $(1, 2)$ gives $(4, 5)$: $4/1 \ne 5/2$.

blocks.hint: Multiply each by $A$, or ask whether it lies on the line through $(1, 1)$ or the line through $(1, -1)$.
blocks.solution: Any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector, with the same eigenvalue. So an eigenvector is really a direction: a whole line through the origin.

blocks.title: A negative multiple
blocks.why: A multiple may be negative. It flips the arrow but keeps the line, and the stretch stays the same.
blocks.prompt: $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $v = (-2, 2)$. Find the eigenvalue $\lambda$ with $Av = \lambda v$.

slips.say: $-2$ is how $v$ relates to $(1, -1)$: $v = -2\,(1, -1)$. The eigenvalue is what $A$ multiplies $v$ by.
3 belongs to the line through $(1, 1)$. Is $(-2, 2)$ on that line?
Check the sign: $A\,(-2, 2)$ has the same signs as $(-2, 2)$.

hints: Row 1 of $A$ dotted with $(-2, 2)$ gives the first entry of $Av$.

check.say: $(-2, 2) = -2\,(1, -1)$. Multiples share an eigenvalue, so you can predict the answer before you multiply.

blocks.solution: $Av = v$, so $\lambda = 1$, the same as for $(1, -1)$. The sign of the multiple does not matter. Next lesson: how to find the eigenvalues without guessing vectors.
